faq.a: Yes. A social animal lives and works with others of its kind, like ants, wolves and elephants. Humans are among the most social animals of all: we live in families, villages, cities and countries.

faq.q: How does a group keep people safe?
faq.a: In a group, many people watch for danger, warn each other and defend each other. Early humans in groups could scare off big animals that would beat one person alone.
Hunting and gathering often fails on a single day. When a group shares, whoever finds food feeds the others, and next time they feed you. Sharing means nobody goes hungry for long.
asks: Why did early humans share food?

faq.q: How do we learn from groups?
faq.a: People pass skills and ideas to each other: how to talk, cook, build and count. Each generation adds a little, so knowledge keeps growing. One person alone could never learn it all.
asks: Why do we learn from others?

faq.q: Why does belonging feel so good?
faq.a: Our brains reward us with good feelings when we are close to others, because for early humans being part of a group meant staying alive. Being left out can feel painful for the same reason.
asks: Why does being left out hurt?

facts: Scientists call humans an "ultra-social" species: we cooperate in larger groups with non-relatives than almost any other mammal.
A 2010 review of 148 studies (Holt-Lunstad and others) found strong social ties linked to about a 50 percent higher chance of survival.
In 2023 the US Surgeon General compared the health risk of loneliness to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.
